title: Cap. VIII Arg. 6: Fathers and Augustine — reprobates must acknowledge justice for their sins
latin: Reprobi monentur, ut in sua reprobatione semper justitiam Divinam agnoscant, qua propter ipsorum peccata merito reprobati fuerunt: Ergo reprobantur ex praevisione demeritorum suorum, in quibus praevidentur hanc suam vitam finitori. Horsum afferuntur multa testimonia ex Patribus, atque nominatim ex ipso Augustino: Quale est illud, De bono persever. cap. 6. Voluntate sua quisque deserit Deum, ut merito deseratur a Deo. Item et illud, De gratia et libero arbitr. cap. 21. Cum legitis in sacris literis obdurari corda hominum, nolite dubitare praecessisse mala merita eorum, ut juste ista paterentur. Et rursus, Ibid. cap. 23. Quando auditis dicentem Dominum, Cujus vult miseretur et quem vult indurat, in eo quem permittit indurari mala ejus merita credite, in eo vero cujus miseretur, Gratiam Dei reddentis bona pro malis indubitanter agnoscite. Denique apertissime hoc asseritur Epistola 105, Quaerimus meritum obdurationis, et invenimus. Merito namque peccati universa massa damnata est, Quibus Deus misericordiam non impertitur, ut non impertatur merentur. Consimilia multa passim occurrunt apud Augustinum et alios Patres, ex quibus concludunt adversarii, Praevisa demerita, cum finali perduratione in iisdem, fuisse causam motivam reprobationis Divinae.
pass_a: The reprobate are warned, that in their reprobation they always acknowledge the Divine justice, by which on account of their own sins they were deservedly reprobated: Therefore they are reprobated from the foresight of their demerits, in which they are foresighted as about to finish this their life. Hither are brought many testimonies from the Fathers, and namely from Augustine himself: Such is that, On the Good of Perseverance chapter 6. By his own will each deserts God, that he may deservedly be deserted by God. Likewise also that, On Grace and Free Will chapter 21. When you read in the sacred letters that the hearts of men are hardened, do not doubt that their evil deserts preceded, that they might justly suffer these things. And again, Ibid. chapter 23. When you hear the Lord saying, He has mercy on whom he will and whom he will he hardens, in him whom he permits to be hardened believe his evil deserts, but in him on whom he has mercy, indubitably acknowledge the Grace of God rendering goods for evils. Finally this is most openly asserted in Epistle 105, We seek the merit of hardening, and we find it. For by desert of sin the universal mass is damned, Those to whom God does not impart mercy merit that it not be imparted. Very many like things everywhere occur in Augustine and other Fathers, from which the adversaries conclude that Foresighted demerits, with final lasting in the same, were the moving cause of Divine reprobation.
pass_b: Sixth: the reprobate are warned always to acknowledge in their reprobation the divine justice by which, for their own sins, they were deservedly reprobated. Therefore, say adversaries, they are reprobated from foresight of the demerits in which they are foresighted as finishing this life. Many Father-testimonies are brought, especially Augustine: On the Good of Perseverance 6 — By his own will each deserts God, that he may deservedly be deserted by God. On Grace and Free Will 21 — When you read in Scripture that men's hearts are hardened, do not doubt their evil deserts went before, that they might justly suffer it. Again, chapter 23 — When you hear the Lord say He has mercy on whom he will and whom he will he hardens, in him whom God permits to be hardened believe his evil deserts; in him on whom God has mercy, acknowledge without doubt the grace that returns goods for evils. Most openly in Epistle 105: We seek the merit of hardening, and we find it. By desert of sin the universal mass is damned; those to whom God does not impart mercy merit that it not be imparted. From many such passages in Augustine and other Fathers, adversaries conclude that foresighted demerits with final lasting in them were the moving cause of divine reprobation.

lemmas.lemma: De bono persever. / De gratia et libero arb.

lemmas.gloss: merit of hardening in the damned mass

title: Cap. VIII Arg. 6 Resp.: negative (Scotus permissive) vs punitive reprobation — if the latter, we grant
latin: Ut haec omnia diluantur, primo in memoriam revocandum est, nos agere de reprobatione illa, quam Theologi vocant negativam; quam Scotus permissivam appellat, in Sentent. lib. 1, dist. 41, quaest. 1; non de illa quam positivam sive punitivam licet appellare. Prior ita considerata dicit solummodo Dei propositum aeternum de non-concedendo singularibus quibusdam personis gratuitum quoddam, indebitum, et speciale beneficium, quo concesso emollirentur, converterentur, et ad vitam aeternam infallibiliter perducerentur. Posterior dicit aeternum Dei propositum de quibusdam personis morte aeterna puniendis ob peccata illa quae perpetrabunt, et a quibus minime liberandi praevidentur. Si ad hoc posterius decretum respiciant adversarii, ultro largimur, hoc aeternum praedamnationis decretum non tendere in quenquam, nisi ea ratione quod peccati reatu constringatur. Nam licet Deus velit servare miseros absque ullis eorum meritis, quia bonus est, non tamen vult damnare aut punire innocentes absque ullis demeritis, quia justus est.
pass_a: That all these may be washed away, first it is to be recalled to memory that we treat of that reprobation which the Theologians call negative; which Scotus calls permissive, in the Sentences book 1, distinction 41, question 1; not of that which it is permitted to call positive or punitive. The former so considered says only the eternal purpose of God concerning not granting to certain singular persons some gratuitous, unowed, and special benefit, which being granted they would be softened, converted, and infallibly led unto eternal life. The latter says the eternal purpose of God concerning certain persons to be punished with eternal death on account of those sins which they will perpetrate, and from which they are foresighted as least to be freed. If the adversaries look to this latter decree, we freely grant that this eternal decree of predamnation tends unto no one, except by that reason that he is bound by the guilt of sin. For although God wills to save the miserable without any merits of theirs, because he is good, yet he does not will to damn or punish innocents without any demerits, because he is just.
pass_b: To clear all this, recall first: we are treating the reprobation theologians call negative — which Scotus calls permissive (Sentences 1, dist. 41, q. 1) — not the positive or punitive kind. Negative reprobation, so taken, means only God's eternal purpose not to grant certain particular persons some gratuitous, unowed, special benefit by which, if granted, they would be softened, converted, and infallibly led to eternal life. Positive reprobation means God's eternal purpose to punish certain persons with eternal death for the sins they will commit, and from which they are foresighted as not to be freed. If adversaries mean that latter decree, we freely grant: the eternal decree of predamnation tends to no one except as bound by sin's guilt. God wills to save the miserable without their merits, because he is good; he does not will to damn or punish innocents without demerits, because he is just.

lemmas.gloss: if punitive, we grant sin's guilt binds

title: Cap. VIII Arg. 6 Resp.: Augustine's just judgment refers to original demerit as adjunct, not motive
latin: Secundo, quando Augustinus affirmat, in reprobatione nos debere agnoscere justum Dei judicium, non id ad praevisa actualia peccata singulorum, sed ad commune debitum originale est referendum. Non igitur juvat eos qui hanc reprobationem a praevisione finalis perseverantiae in actualibus peccatis deducunt. Porro, originalis peccati considerationem in hac reprobatione negativa ita concedimus, ut fuerit adjunctum adhaerens subjecto reprobato, non autem ut fuerit causa movens voluntatem Divinam ad hunc actum reprobandi. Agnoscendum itaque est, hunc actum reprobationis negativae, qua gratia specialis neganda decernitur personae solo peccato originali contaminatae, non sine justitia, multo minus contra justitiam, exerceri. Nam (quod ante annotavimus) satis juste negatur quod ex justitia non debetur; sed interim tenendum, non ex retribuente et vindicante justitia, sed ex libertate Divinae voluntatis, cujus vult miserentis, et quem vult praetereuntis, dependere, quod in communi hoc reatu originalis peccati quidam decernantur efficaciter liberandi, quidam per negationem gratiae specialis in illo statu relinquendi.
pass_a: Secondly, when Augustine affirms that in reprobation we ought to acknowledge the just judgment of God, that is not to be referred unto foresighted actual sins of individuals, but unto the common original debt. It therefore does not help those who deduce this reprobation from the foresight of final perseverance in actual sins. Further, we so concede consideration of original sin in this negative reprobation, that it was an adjunct adhering to the reprobated subject, but not that it was a moving cause of the Divine will unto this act of reprobating. It is therefore to be acknowledged that this act of negative reprobation, by which special grace is decreed to be denied to a person contaminated by original sin alone, is exercised not without justice, much less against justice. For (what we noted before) what is not owed from justice is sufficiently justly denied; but meantime it is to be held that it depends not from retributing and vindicating justice, but from the liberty of the Divine will, having mercy on whom it will, and passing by whom it will, that in this common guilt of original sin certain ones are decreed to be efficaciously freed, certain ones by negation of special grace to be left in that state.
pass_b: Second: when Augustine says that in reprobation we ought to acknowledge God's just judgment, that refers not to foresighted actual sins of individuals, but to the common original debt. So it does not help those who derive this reprobation from foresight of final perseverance in actual sins. We do grant original sin a place in negative reprobation — as an adjunct adhering to the reprobate subject, not as a moving cause of the divine will to that act of reprobating. Negative reprobation, whereby special grace is decreed denied to a person stained by original sin alone, is exercised not without justice, still less against it. What justice does not owe is justly denied; yet the discrimination — some efficaciously freed from this common original guilt, some left in that state by denial of special grace — depends not on retributing and vindicating justice, but on the liberty of the divine will, which has mercy on whom it will and passes by whom it will.

lemmas.gloss: original sin adjunct, not motive of praeterition

title: Cap. VIII Arg. 6 Resp.: negative reprobation not from foresight of final obstinacy; Lombard
latin: Tertio, si contendunt adversarii, hanc reprobationem negativam ex praescientia finalis pertinaciae in actualibus peccatis esse oriundam, respondemus, hoc non modo a veritate sed ab omni verisimilitudine abhorrere. Nam ipsum decretum permittendi finalem hanc obdurationem, in quo sita est reprobatio, absolutam ejusdem obdurationis praescientiam antecedit. Unde Petrus Lombardus, lib. 1, dist. 40, ait, Reprobationem esse praescientiam malitiae in quibusdam et non miserendi. Haec autem praescientia fundatur in decreto negante specialem illam gratiam et de facto cujuscunque cordis quantumvis duri emollientem. Frustra igitur statuitur praescientiam finalem in peccatis permansionem esse reprobationis causam, cum huic finali permansioni praeintelligatur permissio illa, orta ex praevio reprobationis decreto. Haec universe de ipso argumento. Jam sigillatim ad singula testimonia apposita respondebo.
pass_a: Thirdly, if the adversaries contend that this negative reprobation is sprung from foresight of final obstinacy in actual sins, we answer that this abhors not only from truth but from all verisimilitude. For the very decree of permitting this final hardening, in which reprobation is situated, precedes the absolute foresight of the same hardening. Whence Peter Lombard, book 1, distinction 40, says that Reprobation is the foresight of malice in certain ones and of not having mercy. But this foresight is founded in the decree denying that special grace and in fact softening any heart howsoever hard. In vain therefore is it established that foresight of final remaining in sins is the cause of reprobation, since to this final remaining that permission is pre-understood, sprung from the prior decree of reprobation. These things universally concerning the argument itself. Now one by one I will answer unto the singular testimonies set forth.
pass_b: Third: if adversaries claim negative reprobation springs from foresight of final obstinacy in actual sins, that abhors not only truth but all likelihood. The very decree permitting that final hardening — wherein reprobation sits — precedes absolute foresight of the hardening. So Peter Lombard (Sentences 1, dist. 40): Reprobation is foresight of malice in certain ones and of not having mercy. That foresight is founded in the decree denying the special grace that in fact softens any heart, however hard. It is vain, then, to make foresight of final remaining in sins the cause of reprobation, when that remaining presupposes the permission sprung from the prior reprobation decree. So much for the argument in general. Now the testimonies one by one.

lemmas.gloss: reprobation = foresight of malice and not-mercy

title: Cap. VIII Arg. 6 Ad primum: De bono perseverantiae — deserting God concerns common exciting grace
latin: Ad primum: Quando Augustinus dicit, Homines prius deserere Deum, atque inde mereri ut deserantur a Deo, non spectat negationem hujus gratiae, quam efficacem et specialem vocamus, atque in hujus negatione hanc reprobationem sive praeteritionem proprie constitutam asserimus; sed gratiae communioris et excitantis subtractionem; quam fatemur propter demerita tolli hominibus, ita tamen ut sine praevia illa prioris gratiae specialis praeparatione, in hoc contumaciae demeritum incidissent.
pass_a: To the first: When Augustine says that Men first desert God, and thence merit that they be deserted by God, he does not regard the negation of this grace which we call efficacious and special, and in the negation of which we assert this reprobation or passing by to be properly constituted; but the subtraction of a more common and exciting grace; which we confess is taken from men on account of demerits, yet so that without that prior preparation of the prior special grace, they would have fallen into this demerit of contumacy.
pass_b: To the first: when Augustine says men first desert God and thence merit to be deserted by God, he is not speaking of the denial of that efficacious special grace in whose denial we locate reprobation or praeterition proper. He means subtraction of a more common, exciting grace — which we grant is taken from men for demerits — yet so that without the prior preparation of that special grace they would already have fallen into this demerit of contumacy.

lemmas.gloss: De bono persever.: desert precedes desertion

title: Cap. VIII Arg. 6 Ad secundum et tertium: consequent hardening vs eternal will not to soften
latin: Ad secundum et tertium: Quando Augustinus jubet nos credere ejus mala merita non abesse, aut praecessisse, quem Deus indurari permittit, non loquitur de illa aeterna voluntate non-miserendi, non-emolliendi, quae ipsam reprobationem continet, sed de ea obduratione in qua peccator a Deo juste derelictus quasi lapideam quandam duritiem contrahit; quam esse praecedentium peccatorum mercedem haud negamus. Sed hic perpendere oportet, utcunque haec obduratio, quae aucta et provecta consideratur, ut mala dispositio hominis indurati, ex demerito praecedentium peccatorum oriatur, tamen illa prima induratio permissiva, quae consideratur ut sola negatio emollitionis ex parte Dei, non potest oriri ex eodem praeviso demerito. Nam voluntatem non-miserendi, non-emolliendi, in Deo consideratam nasci ex praevisione obdurationis in homine consideratam, aeque absurdum esset ac si quis dixerit diluculum illud solis absentem apud Cimmerios oriri ex praeeunte diuturna obtenebratione aeris.
pass_a: To the second and third: When Augustine bids us believe that his evil deserts are not absent, or preceded, whom God permits to be hardened, he does not speak of that eternal will of not-having-mercy, of not-softening, which contains reprobation itself, but of that hardening in which the sinner justly forsaken by God contracts as it were a certain stony hardness; which we by no means deny to be the wage of preceding sins. But here it is needful to weigh, that howsoever this hardening, considered as increased and advanced, as the evil disposition of the hardened man, arises from the demerit of preceding sins, yet that first permissive hardening, which is considered as the mere negation of softening on God's part, cannot arise from the same foresighted demerit. For that the will of not-having-mercy, of not-softening, considered in God, should be born from foresight of hardening considered in man, would be equally absurd as if someone said that that daylight of the sun absent among the Cimmerians arises from the preceding long darkening of the air.
pass_b: To the second and third: when Augustine bids us believe evil deserts are not absent — or went before — in him whom God permits to be hardened, he is not speaking of that eternal will not to have mercy, not to soften, which contains reprobation itself. He means the hardening in which the sinner, justly forsaken by God, contracts a kind of stony hardness — and we do not deny that is the wage of preceding sins. Weigh this: however much that hardening, taken as increased and advanced as the evil disposition of the hardened man, arises from demerit of preceding sins, the first permissive hardening — mere negation of softening on God's part — cannot arise from that same foresighted demerit. To say God's will not to have mercy, not to soften, is born from foresight of human hardening would be as absurd as saying the sun's daylight, absent among the Cimmerians, arises from the air's long prior darkening.

title: Cap. VIII Arg. 6 Ad ultimum: merit of hardening in original sin; further hardening from daily sins; decree from free will
latin: Ad ultimum testimonium, in quo Augustinus docet facile posse nos invenire in nobis meritum obdurationis, sed meritum misericordiae Divinae non posse invenire, respondeo, loqui illum non de praevisione actualium peccatorum ad finem vitae in hoc vel illo perdurantium, sed de originali peccato, quod est quasi commune demeritum in omnibus Adae filiis, et potest allegari tanquam sufficiens causa, cur Divina misericordia cuivis possit absque omni crudelitatis specie denegari, sed non potest allegari tanquam causa, cur Deus noluerit huic vel illi singulari homini efficax remedium praeparare et adhibere, quo haec ingenita durities edomari posset. Valet igitur originalis peccati consideratio, ut inde inquiras damnationis, sed non eo valet ut inde petatur causa negativae reprobationis. Denique dicuntur omnes reprobi, praesertim qui ad usum liberi arbitrii perveniunt, mereri istam obdurationem, primo, sensu negativo, quia non merentur emollitionem, quia non merentur specialem illam misericordiam; deinde, sensu affirmativo, quia quotidianis suis peccatis merentur illam ulteriorem obdurationem et traditionem εἰς ἀδόκιμον νοῦν, de quo Apostolus Rom. i. 28. Sed interim decretum illud reprobationis, secundum quod permittuntur ita indurescere, dependet ex Dei liberrima voluntate, et non ex praevisa illorum finali duritie; quae utique praevisa esse non potuit, nisi hoc permittendi decreto praesupposito.
pass_a: To the last testimony, in which Augustine teaches that we can easily find in ourselves the merit of hardening, but cannot find the merit of Divine mercy, I answer that he speaks not of the foresight of actual sins lasting unto the end of life in this or that one, but of original sin, which is as it were a common demerit in all the sons of Adam, and can be alleged as a sufficient cause why Divine mercy can be denied to anyone without any appearance of cruelty, but cannot be alleged as a cause why God was unwilling to prepare and apply to this or that singular man an efficacious remedy by which this inborn hardness could be tamed. Consideration of original sin therefore avails that thence you may inquire of damnation, but it does not so avail that thence the cause of negative reprobation be sought. Finally all the reprobate, especially who arrive at the use of free will, are said to merit that hardening, first, in a negative sense, because they do not merit softening, because they do not merit that special mercy; then, in an affirmative sense, because by their daily sins they merit that further hardening and handing over unto a reprobate mind, of which the Apostle Romans 1:28. But meantime that decree of reprobation, according to which they are permitted so to harden, depends from the freest will of God, and not from their foresighted final hardness; which indeed could not be foresighted, unless this decree of permitting were presupposed.
pass_b: To the last testimony — Augustine teaching that we easily find in ourselves the merit of hardening, but cannot find the merit of divine mercy — I answer: he is not speaking of foresight of actual sins lasting to life's end in this or that person, but of original sin, the common demerit of all Adam's children. That can stand as sufficient cause why divine mercy may be denied anyone without any show of cruelty; it cannot stand as cause why God refused to prepare and apply to this or that particular man an efficacious remedy by which that inborn hardness could be tamed. Original sin avails for inquiring into damnation; it does not avail as the cause of negative reprobation. Finally all the reprobate — especially those who reach the use of free will — are said to merit that hardening: negatively, because they do not merit softening or that special mercy; affirmatively, because by daily sins they merit further hardening and handing over to a reprobate mind (Rom. 1:28). Yet the reprobation decree by which they are permitted so to harden depends on God's freest will, not on their foresighted final hardness — which could not be foresighted unless that permitting decree were presupposed.

lemmas.gloss: Ep. 105: find hardening's merit, not mercy's
